topics.title: Equations of Lines
topics.subject: mathematics
outcomes: form linear equations with given points. (k, s)
draw the graph of a line given its equation. (u, s)

body.text: A straight line's equation is usually written y = mx + c, where m is the gradient (how steep the line is) and c is the y-intercept (where the line crosses the y-axis, when x = 0).

To draw the graph of y = 2x + 1, make a table of values: choose a few x values, work out the matching y, then plot the points. When x = 0, y = 1; when x = 1, y = 3; when x = 2, y = 5. Plotting (0, 1), (1, 3) and (2, 5) and joining them with a ruler gives the straight line.

The gradient can also be found from two points already known to be on the line, without an equation to start from: gradient = (change in y) ÷ (change in x). A line through (0, -3) and (2, 1) has gradient (1 - (-3)) ÷ (2 - 0) = 4 ÷ 2 = 2. Since the line crosses the y-axis at (0, -3), c = -3, giving the equation y = 2x - 3.

Lines with the same gradient are parallel — they never meet, because they rise at exactly the same rate. A steeper line has a larger gradient (ignoring sign); a line that slopes downward left-to-right has a negative gradient.
Use the PhET Graphing Lines simulation below to build lines from two points, from a point and a slope, or from the y = mx + c form, and see immediately how changing m or c changes the line.
